title: Salah Chipped a Panenka. Two Australians Missed. Egypt Made History in Dallas.
excerpt: Mohamed Salah fought through a hamstring strain, scored the nerviest penalty of the shootout, and led Egypt to their first-ever World Cup knockout win — a 4-2 shootout victory over Australia in front of 70,244 fans at AT&T Stadium.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Mohamed Salah led Egypt to their first World Cup knockout win against Australia.
  • Egypt won 4-2 on penalties after a 1-1 draw in regulation and extra time.
  • Salah scored a crucial Panenka penalty, showcasing his experience under pressure.
  • Egypt is only the second African nation to win a World Cup penalty shootout.
  • The match drew 70,244 fans at AT&T Stadium in Dallas.
Egypt's Historic Victory
›First World Cup knockout win for Egypt.
›Final score: Egypt 1 - 1 Australia (Egypt won 4-2 on penalties).
›Salah scored the decisive penalty with a Panenka.
›Egypt's second African nation to win a penalty shootout.
›Match attended by 70,244 fans at AT&T Stadium.
Sources: Reuters, The Times (London), USA Today, FIFA

Mohamed Salah was not supposed to start. A hamstring strain suffered during Egypt's final group match against Jordan had cast a shadow over his availability. But when the teams lined up inside AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas on Friday afternoon, there he was — wearing No. 10, positioned on the right, ready for what he later called "the biggest stage you can play on."

He was right about the stage. And about the history.

Egypt beat Australia 4-2 on penalties after a 1-1 draw that stretched through 120 minutes of tension, tactical fouling, and a second-half own goal that briefly threatened to unravel everything Hossam Hassan's side had built.

Ashour's Header, Hany's Nightmare

The Pharaohs struck first. In the 13th minute, Emam Ashour — a midfielder with a defender's instinct for set pieces — rose unmarked to head in Karim Hafez's cross from the left. Jackson Irvine had given away the free kick needlessly, upending Mostafa Zico near the penalty area, and Egypt made him pay.

Australia's response was slow but inevitable. Cristian Volpato's dipping strike clipped the crossbar early, a warning shot. Then, ten minutes into the second half, the equalizer came — and it came from Egypt's own ranks. Mohamed Hany, already responsible for an own goal against Belgium in the group stage, deflected a cross into his own net. His second own goal of the tournament. The Dallas crowd roared.

Omar Marmoush nearly restored Egypt's lead within seconds of the restart, but his close-range shot drifted wide. It was a miss that could have made the shootout unnecessary.

![World Cup — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fb/Kitzbuehel_slalom_ganslernhang_2010.jpg)

Extra Time: Thirty Minutes of Nothing and Everything

> ""If somebody was going to do it, it would be me," Salah said afterward, grinning."

Neither side could find a breakthrough in extra time. Australia brought on veteran goalkeeper Mathew Ryan to replace Patrick Beach for the shootout — a move that carried the weight of experience and desperation in equal measure. Egypt replaced the tiring Marmoush with Hamza Abdelkarim. Both coaches had rolled their dice.

The Shootout

Harry Souttar stepped up first for Australia and blazed his penalty over the bar. From that moment, the arithmetic was Egypt's to lose.

Mahmoud Saber scored. Jackson Irvine converted for Australia. Ramy Rabia slotted home. Awer Mabil leveled it at 2-2.

Then came Salah. He walked to the spot, placed the ball, and chipped a Panenka — the kind of penalty that either makes you immortal or makes you a cautionary tale. Ryan dove. The ball floated gently into the centre of the net.

"If somebody was going to do it, it would be me," Salah said afterward, grinning. "I am more experienced than others and I wanted to give them confidence. I decided last minute — I had to do it."

![The Times — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/e/e1/Thetimespapercover.jpg)

Lucas Herrington, Australia's young substitute, stepped up needing to score. He missed. Hossam Abdelmaguid rolled in the fifth Egyptian penalty, and that was that.

Egypt had won their first-ever World Cup knockout match.

"It's History"

Salah looked close to tears during the celebrations, embracing teammates and coaching staff. No player has created more chances at this World Cup than the former Liverpool forward — 16 across the tournament, level with Belgium's Leandro Trossard — and five of those came in this match alone.

"It's history," he said. "I told the boys before the game that this is the biggest stage you can play on. Enjoy it and don't let the pressure get to you. I'm glad that we managed to win the game. I'm happy that we wrote history today."

Egypt are only the second African nation ever to win a World Cup penalty shootout, after Morocco's two victories — against Spain in 2022 and the Netherlands earlier in this tournament.

What's Next — and Why NRIs Were Watching

Egypt advance to the Round of 16 on Tuesday, July 7, where they will face the winner of Argentina vs Cape Verde — a match that was still being played in Miami as Egyptian fans celebrated in Dallas.

For the Indian diaspora, this match carried layers of relevance. AT&T Stadium sits in the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex, home to one of the largest and fastest-growing Indian-American communities in the United States. NRIs in the DFW area have been living inside this World Cup for weeks — attending matches, filling watch parties, and experiencing the tournament not as distant television but as a neighborhood event.

And for the hundreds of thousands of Indians living in Australia — one of the largest NRI communities outside of North America — the Socceroos' elimination hits closer to home. Australia's World Cup is over. Egypt's, somehow, beautifully, is not.

*Sources: Reuters, The Times (London), USA Today, FIFA*
